title: Edit4D: Editable 4D Scene Generation with Textual Control

paper.title: Edit4D: Editable 4D Scene Generation with Textual Control
paper.abstract:
Abstract We introduce Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D scene generation framework that constructs 4D scenes from separate background and dynamic character representations.
Recent advances in generative models have enabled text-driven dynamic scene synthesis, but editable 4D scene generation remains challenging due to the need to preserve spatial geometry and temporal dynamics.
Existing approaches typically generate holistic scene videos, where the background and dynamic characters are coupled, making object-level editing and flexible camera control difficult.
Edit4D addresses these limitations through a stage-specific generation pipeline.
Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage-specific prompts for background, dynamic character, and scene–character composition.
Using these prompts, we synthesize multi-view scene images with text-to-image and camera-conditioned generative priors and reconstruct a background 3D Gaussian splatting representation.
We then generate a character image, animate it with an image-conditioned video prior, reconstruct a 4D mesh, and bind Gaussian primitives to obtain a character representation.
Finally, both components are composed through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization.
A global scene refinement is then performed to improve harmonization and rendering consistency.
By integrating stage-specific components, Edit4D enables controllable camera motion, flexible object-level editing, and the practical construction of editable 4D scenes.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Advances in large-scale text-to-image models such as DALL-E [ 48 ] and Stable Diffusion [ 51 ] have rapidly accelerated visual content generation. This progress is especially evident in video generation, where models such as Sora [ 36 ] and Veo [ 11 ] demonstrate strong photorealism, temporal coherence, and scene complexity. Building on these advances, recent research has shifted toward 3D and 4D content creation. In particular, 4D generation aims to capture both spatial structure and temporal evolution, requiring multi-view consistency, temporal coherence, and stable 3D geometry. Despite progress in diffusion models, general 4D scene generation remains challenging and has yet to reach the level required for widespread commercial use. Existing text-to-4D methods can be broadly divided into object-level and scene-level approaches. Object-level methods [ 2 , 79 ] often produce multi-view consistent dynamic subjects by focusing on a single foreground object, but they do not generate complete scenes with backgrounds. Scene-level methods [ 75 , 35 ] synthesize complete dynamic scenes as a single holistic representation, making object-level editing difficult. Moreover, because geometry is reconstructed from a limited set of generated viewpoints, rendering quality often degrades under novel-view changes. These challenges are further amplified by the scarcity of large-scale dynamic-scene datasets, which forces many methods to rely on distillation from image or video generative priors. Although such priors provide useful supervision, the resulting 4D content remains constrained by their quality and failure modes. Furthermore, when artifacts appear in the generated content, even localized errors require regenerating the entire sequence, making correction costly and prone to inconsistencies with the original output. In real production workflows, where expert-driven refinement is often necessary, this lack of editability becomes a significant limitation. These observations suggest that constructing 4D scenes as composable assets, rather than as a single monolithic video, offers a more flexible alternative. Asset-based generation naturally aligns with graphics workflows, allowing creators to manipulate and replace scene components with greater control. However, editable 4D scene construction remains underexplored, as existing pipelines often couple backgrounds with dynamic elements and make independent editing difficult. To address these limitations, we introduce Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D framework that constructs 4D scenes from separate background scene and dynamic character representations. Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage-specific prompts for background, dynamic character, and composition. We then generate the 4D scene through parallel background scene and dynamic character generation, followed by scene–character composition. The background scene is reconstructed as a 3D Gaussian representation from multi-view images synthesized using text-to-image and camera-conditioned generative priors. For the dynamic character, we generate a reference video by animating a character image, reconstructing a temporally consistent 4D mesh, and binding Gaussian primitives to obtain a dynamic character representation. The composition stage localizes the target placement region with text-guided masks and optimizes the character pose using contact-aware constraints. We further perform a global scene refinement to improve appearance consistency and rendering details. Extensive experiments show that Edit4D achieves state-of-the-art performance against recent 4D generation methods, while additionally supporting controllable camera motion. We illustrate the overview of our method in Fig. Edit4D: Editable 4D Scene Generation with Textual Control . Figure 2 : Comparison of novel-view renderings from 4D scenes generated by Free4D [ 35 ] and our method. Compared to methods that directly distill video diffusion priors, our composition-based method constructs the 4D scene from explicit background and dynamic 3D components, maintaining better visual quality under novel-view camera changes. We summarize our contributions as follows: • We propose Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D framework that constructs 4D scenes by composing separate background and dynamic character representations through a stage-specific generation pipeline. This component-wise design enables independent editing, flexible control, and scene recomposition within a unified 4D space. • We introduce a text-guided composition method that automatically places a dynamic character into a background scene. Our method localizes target region from text and optimizes character position with contact and penetration constraints, reducing the need for manual placement. • Edit4D achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with recent 4D generation methods while preserving high perceptual quality. Beyond generation quality, it supports camera control and fine-grained object-level editing.

sections.heading: 2.1 3D and 4D Scene Generation
sections.text: Text-to-3D generation has advanced rapidly with the development of large-scale generative models. Score distillation sampling (SDS)-based methods [ 46 , 64 , 8 , 30 , 80 , 31 ] synthesize 3D content by aligning rendered views with text-conditioned diffusion priors, but they are computationally expensive and often suffer from view-dependent artifacts and the Janus problem. Recent multi-view guided methods address these limitations by generating geometrically consistent views and then lifting them into 3D representations. Text-conditioned [ 25 , 53 , 26 , 19 ] and image-conditioned [ 60 , 33 , 32 , 37 , 71 ] approaches follow this paradigm to improve visual fidelity and efficiency. More recently, data-driven models [ 78 , 68 , 57 ] trained on large-scale 3D datasets generate 3D from text or image inputs. Building on these advances, recent text- or video-to-4D methods [ 44 , 49 , 50 , 54 , 56 , 74 , 79 , 2 , 75 , 35 ] synthesize dynamic 3D content using diffusion guidance, multi-view generation, or SDS-based optimization. Object-level methods such as 4Dfy [ 2 ] and Dream-in-4D [ 79 ] can produce temporally coherent and multi-view consistent dynamic objects. Scene-level methods such as 4Real [ 75 ] and Free4D [ 35 ] instead generate complete dynamic scenes, improving photorealism or temporal consistency through video-conditioned reconstruction or point-guided denoising. However, these methods typically perform holistic 4D synthesis, making it difficult to isolate and control individual scene components after generation. In contrast, Edit4D constructs 4D scenes from separate representations, enabling fine-grained modification while preserving spatio-temporal coherence. Figure 3 : Detailed Generation Pipeline of Edit4D. In the first stage, Edit4D decomposes a user instruction into background scene text, character appearance and motion text, and composition text for target placement via off-the-shelf large language model. In the second stage, our framework generates background scene and dynamic character. A background scene is generated as a 3D Gaussian representation using text- and camera-conditioned priors. It then constructs a dynamic 3D character via video-guided mesh reconstruction and Gaussian binding. In the third stage, both components are composed through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization to obtain an editable 4D scene. Finally, we perform a global scene refinement to improve appearance harmonization and rendering consistency.

sections.heading: 2.2 Scene Representation
sections.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [ 38 ] established a foundation for neural 3D scene representations through volumetric rendering. Although NeRF achieves high visual fidelity, its slow rendering speed motivated more efficient variants such as Instant-NGP [ 41 ] and HexPlane [ 5 ] , which leverage hash-based or tensor-decomposed encodings. More recently, Gaussian Splatting [ 22 ] introduced a rasterization-based representation using Gaussian primitives, enabling real-time rendering with high visual quality. This line of work has been extended to dynamic 4D representations, including NeRFPlayer [ 55 ] , 4D-GS [ 66 ] , and Grid4D [ 69 ] , which jointly model spatial structure and temporal motion. However, accurately recovering geometry remains challenging when optimization relies mainly on photometric supervision. Recent methods such as SuGaR [ 13 ] and 2D Gaussian [ 18 ] redesign Gaussian primitives to align with underlying surfaces, while structure-guided frameworks like GaussianAvatar [ 40 , 17 ] and Mani-GS [ 10 ] attach the Gaussians to deformable meshes for stable geometry.

sections.heading: 2.3 Scene Composition
sections.text: With recent advances in segmentation foundation models [ 23 , 76 ] , mask-based composition methods in 3D neural scenes have been actively studied. By leveraging 2D masks from segmentation or text-to-mask models, prior methods localize editable regions for object removal and inpainting, ensuring reliable composition [ 3 , 73 , 52 ] . More closely related to our work, human-scene placement methods aim to place human in 3D scene with physically plausible contact while reducing interpenetration artifacts. PROX [ 14 ] fits SMPL-X [ 45 ] bodies to scenes using contact and penetration constraints, and POSA [ 15 ] learns a body-centric contact representation for plausible placements. Furthermore, COINS [ 77 ] and Narrator [ 70 ] refine using contact optimization to encourage natural human-scene contact. However, these methods typically assume reconstructed real scenes, supervised interaction data, or manually prepared assets. In contrast, Edit4D performs text-driven scene–character composition, allowing dynamic characters to be automatically placed into generated background scenes through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We propose Edit4D, a unified framework for generating editable 4D scenes from textual descriptions. As shown in Fig. 3 , our framework composes independently generated background scenes and dynamic characters into a unified 4D representation, enabling object-level editing and recomposition. We first describe our editable 4D scene representation based on Gaussian splatting. We then explain how Edit4D constructs a 4D scene through a stage-specific generation pipeline using off-the-shelf generative priors.

sections.heading: 3.2 Stage 1: Instruction Decomposition
sections.text: Edit4D takes a single user instruction that describes the background scene, dynamic character, and scene–character composition. Since each module requires different information, the original instruction is not directly suitable for all stages of the pipeline. We therefore use a large language model [ 42 ] to convert the user instruction into stage-specific prompts while preserving its original semantics. As shown in Fig. 3 , the decomposed prompts guide background scene generation, dynamic 3D character generation, and scene–character composition. This instruction decomposition allows each module to operate with an appropriate prompt and enables the overall pipeline to run automatically from a single user instruction.

sections.heading: 3.3 Stage 2: Background Scene Generation
sections.text: To generate a background scene, we first synthesize a high-quality scene image from the background scene text. This image serves as a reference that defines the overall layout, appearance, and semantic structure of the scene. We then employ a camera-conditioned multi-view generation model to expand the image into a set of geometrically consistent views along sampled camera trajectories. These generated views provide additional spatial observations and parallax cues necessary for reliable 3D reconstruction. Finally, we reconstruct a background Gaussian splatting representation from the generated multi-view observations, yielding a globally consistent background representation 𝒢 bg \mathcal{G}^{\text{bg}} .

sections.heading: 3.4 Stage 2: Dynamic 3D Character Generation
sections.text: We use a text-to-image model to generate a character image and animate it with the image-conditioned video generator. Given the generated video, we employ a mesh estimator [ 7 ] to reconstruct a deformable mesh sequence { 𝐌 t } t = 1 T \{\mathbf{M}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} with temporally consistent topology across time. To enable joint rendering with the background scene, we convert the mesh sequence into a 4D Gaussian splatting representation using the mesh-binding scheme following [ 10 ] to exploit mesh topology. Specifically, Gaussians are attached to mesh faces and updated according to the underlying mesh deformation, providing a topology-aware dynamic representation. sections.heading: 3.6 Global Scene Refinement
sections.text: Although the proposed composition stage produces physically plausible scene–character composition, appearance discrepancies may still remain between the independently generated background and character. Unlike the composition stage, which only updates the character pose, we jointly optimize the background scene, canonical character Gaussians, and the deformation field. This refinement encourages appearance harmonization between independently generated components while improving fine-grained visual details. For dynamics, we only use the frontal view to preserve character identity and temporal consistency during optimization. Furthermore, we improve scene–character consistency by generating cast shadows based on the estimated scene illumination. We estimate an HDR environment map from background multi-view renderings [ 29 ] and compute character-induced light occlusion following Gaussian ray tracing [ 39 , 12 ] . The resulting attenuation is applied to the rendered background, producing temporally consistent cast shadows that follow the scene illumination. sections.heading: 4.1 Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: Following the evaluation protocol of Free4D [ 35 ] , we evaluate all methods using frontal-view videos from publicly available examples. We use three VBench [ 20 ] metrics. First, Text Align measures semantic similarity between generated videos and input prompts using ViClip [ 63 ] video-text embeddings. Consistency measures temporal coherence of subjects and backgrounds using DINO [ 6 ] and CLIP [ 47 ] feature similarities. Finally, Aesthetic evaluates visual quality using the LAION Aesthetic Predictor [ 24 ] , which considers factors such as layout, harmony, photorealism, and overall artistic impression. sections.heading: 4.3 Qualitative Results
sections.text: We compare our method with 4Real [ 75 ] , Dream-in-4D [ 79 ] , 4Dfy [ 2 ] and Free4D [ 35 ] in Fig. 4 . Despite generating scene components independently, Edit4D produces coherent and natural 4D scenes with visual quality comparable to existing methods. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 5 , we also render the 4D scene from four novel viewpoints over time. Compared with the previous method [ 35 ] , our approach maintains more stable visual quality under large camera motions, demonstrating the effectiveness of our framework that constructs the 4D scene from independently generated components.

sections.heading: 4.4 Evaluation on Editability
sections.text: We evaluate the editability of our method through scene–character recomposition and character appearance editing. For comparison, Free4D requires full regeneration because it represents the scene holistically. Therefore, we generate the edited reference videos using the same model, and execute the released Free4D code. Since the goal of editing is to modify the target component while preserving the rest of the scene, we define editing success based on the preservation of the original background scene. We assess this using three VLMs [ 59 , 58 , 1 ] . Moreover, we measure background preservation using CLIP [ 47 ] and DINO [ 43 ] similarities after masking the character regions. For the editing evaluation, we additionally conduct a user study to assess how well the remaining scene content is preserved after editing. As shown in Tab. 3 , Edit4D achieves higher editing success and background preservation while reducing editing time. In Fig. 6 , Free4D shows noticeable changes in background content, such as the bookshelf and rug, due to full regeneration, whereas Edit4D preserves the original scene more consistently. This efficiency comes from our asset based representation, which reuses components instead of regenerating the entire 4D scene. sections.heading: 4.5 Ablation Study
sections.text: We conduct ablation studies to analyze how each component of Edit4D affects scene–character composition and 4D generation quality. Tab. 4 shows that removing initialization, contact loss, penetration loss, and global refinement degrades different metrics, while the full model achieves the best quantitative results. Fig. 7 further visualizes the effect of each composition component. Without initialization, the optimization often converges to an incorrect placement, whereas removing the contact loss causes the character to float above the support surface, and removing the penetration loss results in penetration into the scene geometry. These results indicate that each constraint and refinement provide complementary benefits for robust placement, visual quality, and scene coherence. Moreover, Fig. 8 demonstrates the effect of the global refinement stage. The refinement stage enhances fine-grained details while improving the overall visual coherence of the composed 4D scene.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we presented Edit4D, a framework for editable 4D scene generation that separates background scenes and dynamic characters for object-level control and composition. Quantitative evaluations on VBench demonstrate state-of-the-art generation quality, while our editability evaluation shows that Edit4D better preserves unedited scene content and reduces editing time compared with holistic regeneration. Qualitative results further demonstrate that Edit4D produces coherent 4D scenes and remains robust under large camera viewpoint changes, supporting reliable novel-view synthesis and dynamic camera control. Our analysis validates the effectiveness of text-guided composition and contact-aware optimization for semantically and physically plausible character placement. Together, these results show that Edit4D provides a practical and flexible framework for high-quality editable 4D scene generation. sections.heading: Appendix A Implementation details
sections.text: We describe the implementation of Edit4D by summarizing each component: instruction decomposition, background scene generation, dynamic 3D character generation, scene–character composition, and global scene refinement. Importantly, Edit4D is not tied to the specific pretrained models used in our implementation. Each stage is modular and can be replaced by an alternative model with compatible input and output representations, allowing the framework to incorporate different open-source models without changing the overall pipeline.

sections.heading: A.1 Instruction Decomposition
sections.text: We use GPT v5.2 [ 42 ] to decompose a user instruction into stage-specific prompts for background scene generation, character generation, motion generation, and scene–character composition. Each prompt contains only the information required by its corresponding stage, allowing the pipeline to operate automatically from a single user instruction while preventing unnecessary information from being propagated across stages. The instruction template is summarized in Table 5 .

sections.heading: A.2 Background Scene Generation
sections.text: Given a textual scene description, we first synthesize a frontal background scene image ( 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 ) using a text-to-image model [ 65 ] . To enable 3D reconstruction, we then generate a set of geometrically consistent multi-view images by extending the frontal view to additional camera poses via a multi-view generation framework. The resulting multi-view set is used to estimate a 3D Gaussian splatting representation of the background. In our implementation, we use VistaDream [ 62 ] to jointly produce trajectory-conditioned multi-view inpainting images and reconstruct the background Gaussian splatting in a unified pipeline.

sections.heading: A.3 Dynamic 3D Character Generation
sections.text: We generate a dynamic character in five steps: (1) image generation, (2) image-conditioned video generation, (3) 4D mesh estimation, (4) multi-view rendering, and (5) training dynamic Gaussian splatting. We first synthesize a character image ( 800 × 800 800\times 800 ) from a text prompt, and then generate an image-aligned motion video ( 800 × 800 800\times 800 , 60 frames) using an image- and text-conditioned video model [ 61 ] . The temporally consistent 4D mesh sequence is reconstructed using Motion 3-to-4 [ 7 ] , which estimates a canonical reference mesh and predicts per-frame vertex trajectories to recover temporally coherent geometry. To render the character together with the Gaussian splatting background efficiently, we convert the 4D mesh to a dynamic Gaussian representation. Specifically, we render multi-view images in Blender [ 4 ] using 30 cameras uniformly distributed on a sphere and bind Gaussian primitives to mesh faces following Mani-GS [ 10 ] , so that Gaussians follow mesh deformations over time. To further improve temporal stability under non-rigid deformation, we incorporate a lightweight deformation field following [ 72 ] that predicts per-time offsets of Gaussian position, rotation, scale, and color. We execute all of the image and video generation steps in ComfyUI [ 9 ] . Moreover, to improve generation quality, we additionally employ task-specific positive and negative prompts to suppress common generation artifacts (e.g., shadows, background leakage, and watermark-like artifacts).

sections.heading: A.4 Scene–Character Composition
sections.text: Given the background and dynamic character Gaussians, we optimize a single global rigid transform of the character, parameterized by a global rotation and translation. The rotation is applied around the character center, followed by translation, while the character scale is fixed to a predefined value between 0.6 and 1.2. We initialize the character position using the bounding boxes of the character mesh and the target Gaussians. Specifically, we first align the character center with the center of the target region. Following the y y -down coordinate convention, we then apply a small offset along the negative y y -axis to place the character slightly above the support surface before optimization. This initialization provides a stable starting point for subsequent contact-aware optimization. Next, we minimize a weighted sum of contact and penetration losses for 1000 iterations: ℒ composition = λ contact ​ ℒ contact + λ penetration ​ ℒ penetration . \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{composition}}=\lambda_{\text{contact}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{contact}}+\lambda_{\text{penetration}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{penetration}}. (11) In our experiments, we set λ contact = 10 2 \lambda_{\text{contact}}=10^{2} and λ penetration = 10 4 \lambda_{\text{penetration}}=10^{4} , assigning a stronger penalty to interpenetration. For the penetration loss, we precompute a signed distance field (SDF) from the character mesh on a 128 3 128^{3} grid with a padding of 0.05 0.05 , where negative SDF values indicate points inside the character mesh. During optimization, scene points are transformed into the character coordinate system and queried against the SDF using trilinear interpolation. Points with negative SDF values are penalized to discourage interpenetration. The optimized global transform is then applied consistently to the dynamic character Gaussians across all frames.

sections.heading: A.6 Runtime
sections.text: On a single RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU, Edit4D takes on average approximately 2 hours per example: 10 minutes for static scene generation, 70 minutes for dynamic character generation, 1 minute for composition, and 45 minutes for global scene refinement. This staged design enables component-level editing of the background scene, dynamic character, and their composition, which is difficult in holistic video-to-4D pipelines. We also compare the runtime of prior text-to-4D methods with publicly available code when generating the same number of frames as Edit4D. 4D-fy and Dream-in-4D typically require more than 24 hours per example due to expensive computation of radiance field and score distillation sampling-based optimization, while Free4D takes approximately 3 hours when including multi-view video generation and 4D Gaussian optimization. More importantly, when editing an existing scene, holistic 4D generation pipelines generally require regenerating the entire 4D result from scratch. Edit4D can instead reuse pre-generated background and character assets, requiring only scene-character composition and optional global scene refinement. This substantially reduces the cost of iterative editing and makes Edit4D a more practical framework for controllable 4D scene creation. sections.heading: Appendix D Details on User Study
sections.text: We conducted an anonymous pairwise user study comparing Edit4D with Free4D [ 35 ] . A total of 25 participants evaluated the rendered 4D scenes through a web-based interface, where the two methods were presented as Video A and Video B without revealing the method names. The scene order and the left–right placement of the two methods were randomized to reduce presentation bias. For a fair comparison, we regenerated the Free4D results using its publicly available implementation. Since Free4D requires a reference video, we generated the corresponding inputs using the same Qwen [ 58 ] and WAN [ 61 ] based generation pipeline used for Edit4D, with the same video resolution and frame setting. Both methods were rendered from multiple viewpoints for comparison. For the original 4D scenes, participants compared 13 scenes and answered two questions regarding 3D Structure and Visual Quality. Specifically, participants selected which result better preserved the perceived 3D structure of the scene and which result appeared visually better. We additionally evaluated editability using five scenes for both scene–character recomposition and character appearance editing. For each method, participants were shown the result before and after editing and asked which method better preserved the background content after the edit. An example of the evaluation interface is shown in Fig. 9 . Figure 10 : Qualitative examples used in the editability evaluation. We compare Free4D and Edit4D for scene–character recomposition and character appearance editing, showing both frontal and rotated views. Free4D requires full scene regeneration for each edit, whereas Edit4D reuses the existing scene assets and better preserves the unedited background content across viewpoints.

sections.heading: Appendix E Evaluation on Editability
sections.text: We further evaluate the editability of Edit4D through character appearance editing and scene–character recomposition. We compare against Free4D, which, to our knowledge, is the only scene-level text-to-4D generation method with publicly available source code, allowing us to directly reproduce its pipeline for controlled editing comparisons. Since Free4D represents the scene holistically, each edit requires full regeneration of the 4D scene. For a fair comparison, we generate the edited reference videos using the same video generation model as Edit4D and run Free4D using its publicly released implementation and settings. Our evaluation focuses on how well the unedited background is preserved after editing. We evaluate five character scenes for each of the two editing tasks and compare the original and edited renderings across multiple camera viewpoints and time steps shown in Fig. 10 . To prevent changes in character position, scale, or appearance from affecting the evaluation, we localize the character using Grounding DINO [ 34 ] and apply a shared mask covering the union of the character regions in the original and edited images. Thus, the evaluation measures the consistency of the background outside the edited region. We assess editing success using three VLMs, GLM-4.6 [ 59 ] , Qwen3-VL [ 58 ] , and Mistral-3.1 [ 1 ] , based on whether the original background scene is preserved after editing. Their decisions are aggregated across sampled viewpoints and time steps. We separately measure background preservation using CLIP [ 47 ] and DINOv2 [ 43 ] similarities computed between the masked original and edited images, where higher similarity indicates better preservation of the unedited background. As reported in the main paper, Edit4D consistently achieves higher editing success and background preservation than Free4D for both editing tasks while requiring substantially less editing time. sections.heading: Appendix F Additional qualitative results
sections.text: We provide additional qualitative results to further demonstrate the editing capability and flexibility of Edit4D. As shown in Fig. 11 , Edit4D supports asset insertion, scene–character recomposition, and character appearance modification using the scene presented in the main paper. In the asset insertion example, we manually place a hat represented as a Gaussian Splatting asset onto the character. Scene–character recomposition is performed by specifying “left sofa” as the target region and repositioning the character through our composition framework. To modify the character appearance, we construct a 3D mask for “cloth” using our masking method and update the color values within the masked region. Since the background and character are represented as reusable 3D assets, these edits can be performed while preserving the remaining scene content without regenerating the entire 4D scene. We further demonstrate the flexibility of our scene–character composition framework in Fig. 12 . As shown in Fig. 12 , our framework can incorporate alternative dynamic character representations. Specifically, we integrate Animatable Gaussians [ 28 ] and obtain plausible multi-character compositions, while visualizing left, center, and right floor masks for controllable placement. To maximize compatibility with diverse character representations, our main pipeline adopts a video-to-mesh model that does not rely on explicit rigging or skeleton annotations. Fig. 12 further presents a more challenging interaction with a large contact area between the character and the scene. For non-contact interactions such as hovering or flying, we replace the contact objective with a distance-thresholded variant that maintains a target distance from the scene surface. As shown in Fig. 12 , this produces stable and non-intersecting floating characters within the same optimization framework. Together, these results demonstrate that the proposed composition framework can accommodate diverse character representations, contact configurations, and spatial relationships. In addition, we present additional generation results across diverse text prompts in Fig. 13 , showing that Edit4D consistently produces coherent and visually plausible 4D scenes. Furthermore, Fig. 14 provides additional novel-view renderings, demonstrating that our method maintains high visual quality under large camera viewpoint changes. sections.text: We visualize the contact intensity map produced by our composition stage in Fig. 15 . Given a composition text, Edit4D first localizes the corresponding target region in the generated background scene and then optimizes the character placement using contact-aware constraints. The high-contact regions align well with the target area specified by the composition text, showing that Edit4D can localize target placement regions and establish plausible character-scene contact. In addition, the character contact maps show that the contact response is mainly activated around physically plausible support regions, such as the lower body or contact-facing surface of the character. Overall, these analyses demonstrate that Edit4D enables physically plausible scene–character composition while maintaining the editability and rendering quality of the generated 4D scene. sections.heading: Appendix H Limitations
sections.text: Our scene–character composition relies on text-guided segmentation to identify the target region for character placement. Therefore, the target object should be sufficiently visible and spatially localized in the input scene. Fig. 16 shows a representative failure case in which the target chair is partially occluded by the desk. Although the visible chair region can be identified, the incomplete target region leads to inaccurate character placement and intersection with the surrounding desk geometry. This limitation could be alleviated by incorporating stronger 3D scene understanding or occlusion-aware target completion into the composition process. Our pipeline also relies on several pretrained modules for intermediate predictions. Errors from these components can propagate to the final 4D scene. For example, imperfect dynamic character reconstruction may introduce temporal or geometric inconsistencies, while inaccurate text-guided segmentation can lead to errors in target localization and composition. Similarly, artifacts in the generated image or reference video can affect the quality of the reconstructed scene or character. Although our refinement stage can alleviate moderate inconsistencies, severe upstream errors may still remain in the final result. Improving robustness to such intermediate prediction errors remains an important direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix I Future Work
sections.text: Edit4D opens several directions for extending editable 4D scene generation. One promising direction is to incorporate more diverse editable assets into the component-wise representation. Since Edit4D constructs background scenes and dynamic characters as separate 3D components, these assets can be inserted or reused across different compositions. Another useful extension is interactive control over scene–character composition, where users can refine placement, contact regions, and spatial relationships after generation. Improving target localization under occlusion through stronger 3D scene understanding or target completion could further increase the robustness of composition. In addition, reducing sensitivity to errors in text-guided segmentation, dynamic character reconstruction, and generated reference images or videos would improve consistency in challenging cases. These directions would further connect text-driven 4D generation with practical graphics-based editing workflows.

Existing approaches typically generate holistic scene videos, where the background and dynamic characters are coupled, making object-level editing and flexible camera control difficult. Edit4D addresses these limitations through a stage-specific generation pipeline. Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage-specific prompts for background, dynamic character, and scene–character composition. Using these prompts, we synthesize multi-view scene images with text-to-image and camera-conditioned generative priors and reconstruct a background 3D Gaussian splatting representation. We then generate a character image, animate it with an image-conditioned video prior, reconstruct a 4D mesh, and bind Gaussian primitives to obtain a character representation. Finally, both components are composed through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization. A global scene refinement is then performed to improve harmonization and rendering consistency. Project page: https://chanwo0kim.github.io/Edit4D/ Figure 1. Overview of Edit4D. Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage-specific prompts. Each stage of the pipeline then takes the corresponding prompts for the scene, character appearance, and motion, and generates the corresponding Gaussian splatting for each stage. We further propose a composition stage that naturally places the character into the background and renders them jointly. By constructing the scene from separated background and dynamic components, Edit4D enables flexible and independent editing. 1 Introduction Advances in large-scale text-to-image models such as DALL-E [ 48 ] and Stable Diffusion [ 51 ] have rapidly accelerated visual content generation. This progress is especially evident in video generation, where models such as Sora [ 36 ] and Veo [ 11 ] demonstrate strong photorealism, temporal coherence, and scene complexity. Building on these advances, recent research has shifted toward 3D and 4D content creation. In particular, 4D generation aims to capture both spatial structure and temporal evolution, requiring multi-view consistency, temporal coherence, and stable 3D geometry. Despite progress in diffusion models, general 4D scene generation remains challenging and has yet to reach the level required for widespread commercial use. Existing text-to-4D methods can be broadly divided into object-level and scene-level approaches. Object-level methods [ 2 , 79 ] often produce multi-view consistent dynamic subjects by focusing on a single foreground object, but they do not generate complete scenes with backgrounds. Scene-level methods [ 75 , 35 ] synthesize complete dynamic scenes as a single holistic representation, making object-level editing difficult. Moreover, because geometry is reconstructed from a limited set of generated viewpoints, rendering quality often degrades under novel-view changes. These challenges are further amplified by the scarcity of large-scale dynamic-scene datasets, which forces many methods to rely on distillation from image or video generative priors. Although such priors provide useful supervision, the resulting 4D content remains constrained by their quality and failure modes. Furthermore, when artifacts appear in the generated content, even localized errors require regenerating the entire sequence, making correction costly and prone to inconsistencies with the original output. In real production workflows, where expert-driven refinement is often necessary, this lack of editability becomes a significant limitation. These observations suggest that constructing 4D scenes as composable assets, rather than as a single monolithic video, offers a more flexible alternative. Asset-based generation naturally aligns with graphics workflows, allowing creators to manipulate and replace scene components with greater control. However, editable 4D scene construction remains underexplored, as existing pipelines often couple backgrounds with dynamic elements and make independent editing difficult. To address these limitations, we introduce Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D framework that constructs 4D scenes from separate background scene and dynamic character representations. Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage-specific prompts for background, dynamic character, and composition. We then generate the 4D scene through parallel background scene and dynamic character generation, followed by scene–character composition. The background scene is reconstructed as a 3D Gaussian representation from multi-view images synthesized using text-to-image and camera-conditioned generative priors. For the dynamic character, we generate a reference video by animating a character image, reconstructing a temporally consistent 4D mesh, and binding Gaussian primitives to obtain a dynamic character representation. The composition stage localizes the target placement region with text-guided masks and optimizes the character pose using contact-aware constraints. We further perform a global scene refinement to improve appearance consistency and rendering details. Extensive experiments show that Edit4D achieves state-of-the-art performance against recent 4D generation methods, while additionally supporting controllable camera motion. We illustrate the overview of our method in Fig. Edit4D: Editable 4D Scene Generation with Textual Control . Figure 2 : Comparison of novel-view renderings from 4D scenes generated by Free4D [ 35 ] and our method. Compared to methods that directly distill video diffusion priors, our composition-based method constructs the 4D scene from explicit background and dynamic 3D components, maintaining better visual quality under novel-view camera changes. We summarize our contributions as follows: • We propose Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D framework that constructs 4D scenes by composing separate background and dynamic character representations through a stage-specific generation pipeline. This component-wise design enables independent editing, flexible control, and scene recomposition within a unified 4D space. • We introduce a text-guided composition method that automatically places a dynamic character into a background scene. Our method localizes target region from text and optimizes character position with contact and penetration constraints, reducing the need for manual placement. • Edit4D achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with recent 4D generation methods while preserving high perceptual quality. Beyond generation quality, it supports camera control and fine-grained object-level editing. 2 Related Works 2.1 3D and 4D Scene Generation Text-to-3D generation has advanced rapidly with the development of large-scale generative models. Score distillation sampling (SDS)-based methods [ 46 , 64 , 8 , 30 , 80 , 31 ] synthesize 3D content by aligning rendered views with text-conditioned diffusion priors, but they are computationally expensive and often suffer from view-dependent artifacts and the Janus problem. Recent multi-view guided methods address these limitations by generating geometrically consistent views and then lifting them into 3D representations. Text-conditioned [ 25 , 53 , 26 , 19 ] and image-conditioned [ 60 , 33 , 32 , 37 , 71 ] approaches follow this paradigm to improve visual fidelity and efficiency. More recently, data-driven models [ 78 , 68 , 57 ] trained on large-scale 3D datasets generate 3D from text or image inputs. Building on these advances, recent text- or video-to-4D methods [ 44 , 49 , 50 , 54 , 56 , 74 , 79 , 2 , 75 , 35 ] synthesize dynamic 3D content using diffusion guidance, multi-view generation, or SDS-based optimization. Object-level methods such as 4Dfy [ 2 ] and Dream-in-4D [ 79 ] can produce temporally coherent and multi-view consistent dynamic objects. Scene-level methods such as 4Real [ 75 ] and Free4D [ 35 ] instead generate complete dynamic scenes, improving photorealism or temporal consistency through video-conditioned reconstruction or point-guided denoising. However, these methods typically perform holistic 4D synthesis, making it difficult to isolate and control individual scene components after generation. In contrast, Edit4D constructs 4D scenes from separate representations, enabling fine-grained modification while preserving spatio-temporal coherence. Finally, we perform a global scene refinement to improve appearance harmonization and rendering consistency. 2.2 Scene Representation Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [ 38 ] established a foundation for neural 3D scene representations through volumetric rendering. Although NeRF achieves high visual fidelity, its slow rendering speed motivated more efficient variants such as Instant-NGP [ 41 ] and HexPlane [ 5 ] , which leverage hash-based or tensor-decomposed encodings. More recently, Gaussian Splatting [ 22 ] introduced a rasterization-based representation using Gaussian primitives, enabling real-time rendering with high visual quality. This line of work has been extended to dynamic 4D representations, including NeRFPlayer [ 55 ] , 4D-GS [ 66 ] , and Grid4D [ 69 ] , which jointly model spatial structure and temporal motion. However, accurately recovering geometry remains challenging when optimization relies mainly on photometric supervision. Recent methods such as SuGaR [ 13 ] and 2D Gaussian [ 18 ] redesign Gaussian primitives to align with underlying surfaces, while structure-guided frameworks like GaussianAvatar [ 40 , 17 ] and Mani-GS [ 10 ] attach the Gaussians to deformable meshes for stable geometry. 2.3 Scene Composition With recent advances in segmentation foundation models [ 23 , 76 ] , mask-based composition methods in 3D neural scenes have been actively studied. By leveraging 2D masks from segmentation or text-to-mask models, prior methods localize editable regions for object removal and inpainting, ensuring reliable composition [ 3 , 73 , 52 ] . More closely related to our work, human-scene placement methods aim to place human in 3D scene with physically plausible contact while reducing interpenetration artifacts. PROX [ 14 ] fits SMPL-X [ 45 ] bodies to scenes using contact and penetration constraints, and POSA [ 15 ] learns a body-centric contact representation for plausible placements. Furthermore, COINS [ 77 ] and Narrator [ 70 ] refine using contact optimization to encourage natural human-scene contact. However, these methods typically assume reconstructed real scenes, supervised interaction data, or manually prepared assets. In contrast, Edit4D performs text-driven scene–character composition, allowing dynamic characters to be automatically placed into generated background scenes through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization. 3 Method We propose Edit4D, a unified framework for generating editable 4D scenes from textual descriptions. As shown in Fig. 3 , our framework composes independently generated background scenes and dynamic characters into a unified 4D representation, enabling object-level editing and recomposition. The refinement stage enhances fine-grained details while improving the overall visual coherence of the composed 4D scene. 5 Conclusion In this work, we presented Edit4D, a framework for editable 4D scene generation that separates background scenes and dynamic characters for object-level control and composition. Quantitative evaluations on VBench demonstrate state-of-the-art generation quality, while our editability evaluation shows that Edit4D better preserves unedited scene content and reduces editing time compared with holistic regeneration. Qualitative results further demonstrate that Edit4D produces coherent 4D scenes and remains robust under large camera viewpoint changes, supporting reliable novel-view synthesis and dynamic camera control. Our analysis validates the effectiveness of text-guided composition and contact-aware optimization for semantically and physically plausible character placement. Together, these results show that Edit4D provides a practical and flexible framework for high-quality editable 4D scene generation.
